¶
'''berycoid''' (ber′i-koid), ''a.'' and ''n.'' '''I.''' ''a.'' Pertaining to the superfamily ''Berycoidea'' or family ''Berycidæ.''

'''II.''' ''n.'' Same as ''berycid.''

'''Berycoidea''' (ber-i-koi′dẹ̄-ä̤), ''n. pl.'' [NL., < ''Beryx'' (''Beryc-'') + ''-oidea.''] A superfamily of acanthopterygian fishes having nearly the same limits as the group ''Beryciformes'', and including the families ''Berycidæ, Monocentridæ, Stephanoberycidæ'', and ''Holocentridæ.''

'''beryl''' (ber′il), ''n.'' [Early mod. E. ''beril, berel, berrel'', etc., < ME. ''beryl, beril, berel'', < OF. ''beril'', < L. ''beryllus, berillus'', < Gr. βήρυλλος, beryl, perhaps < Skt. ''vaidūrya'' (with lingual ''d''), beryl. Cf. Ar. Pers. ''ballūr, bellaur'', crystal.] A colorless, bluish, pinkish, yellow, or more commonly green mineral, occurring in hexagonal prisms.
{{smaller block|The precious emerald is a variety which owes its beauty of color to the presence of a small amount of chromium. See ''emerald.'' Aquamarine is a pale-green transparent variety, also used as a gem, though not highly prized. Beryl is a silicate of aluminium and beryllium (glucinum). The best beryls are found in Brazil and Ceylon, and in Transbaikalia and elsewhere in Siberia. Beryls occur also in many parts of the United States, especially in the New England States and North Carolina; the latter State has afforded some good emeralds.}}

'''beryllia''' (be-ril′i-ä̤), ''n.'' [NL., < ''beryllium.''] Same as ''glucina.''

¶
'''Beryllian''' (be-ril′ian), ''n.'' One of a sect founded in the third century by Beryllus, bishop of Bostra in Arabia, who taught that Christ was non-existent previous to his incarnation, and that at his birth a portion of the divine nature entered into him.

'''berylline''' (ber′i-lin), ''a.'' [< ''beryl'' + ''-ine''<sup>1</sup>.] Like a beryl; of a light- or bluish-green color.

'''beryllium''' (be-ril′i-um), ''n.'' [NL., < Gr. βηρύλλιον, dim. of βήρυλλος, beryl.] Same as ''glucinum''.

'''berylloid''' (ber′i-loid), ''n.'' [< ''beryl'' + ''-oid''.] A solid consisting of two twelve-sided pyramids placed base to base: so called because the planes of this form are common in crystals of beryl.

'''Berytidæ''' (be-rit′i-dē), ''n. pl.'' [NL., < ''Berytus'' + ''-idæ''.] A family of heteropterous insects, containing the most aberrant bugs of the series ''Coreoidea''.

'''Berytus''' (be-rī′tus), ''n.'' [NL.] A genus of hemipterous insects, typical of the family ''Berytidæ''.

'''Beryx''' (ber′iks), ''n.'' [NL.] A genus of percoid fishes, typical of the family ''Berycidæ''.

'''berzelianite''' (bėr-zē′lian-īt), ''n.'' [< ''Berzelian'' (< ''Berzelius'', a celebrated Swedish chemist, 1779–1848) + ''-ite''<sup>2</sup>.] A rare selenide of copper, found in thin incrustations of a silver-white color.

'''berzeliite''' (bėr-zē′li-īt), ''n.'' [< ''Berzelius'' (see ''berzelianite'') + ''-ite''<sup>2</sup>.] An arseniate of calcium, magnesium, and manganese occurring in

'''berzeline''' (bėr′ze-lin), ''n.'' [< ''Berzelius'' (see ''berzelianite'') + ''-ine''<sup>2</sup>.] '''1.''' The copper selenide usually called ''berzelianite.''—'''2.''' A name early given to the mineral haüyne.

'''bes''' (bes), ''n.'' [L., rarely ''bessis'' (''bess-''), < ''bi-'', two-, + ''as'' (''ass-''), as, unit: see ''as''<sup>4</sup>.] In ''Rom. metrology'', two thirds of a unit or eight twelfths of an as; especially, eight cyathi or two thirds of a sextarius; also, the name of a small copper coin. Also ''bessis.''

'''besa''' (bē′sä), ''n.'' [Heb.] A measure of capacity mentioned in rabbinical writings, equal to about one sixth of a United States pint.

'''besabol''' (bes′ạ-bol), ''n.'' [Ar.] A fragrant resinous balsam obtained from a burseraceous tree, ''Commiphora kataf'', of the Somali country in eastern Africa. {{smaller|It was formerly called ''East Indian myrrh'', and differs from true myrrh chiefly in its odor. Also ''bissabol.''}}

'''besagne''' (be-sān′), ''n.'' [OF. ''besange'' (Roquefort), a piece, bit; perhaps same as OF. ''besant'', bezant: see ''bezant.''] In medieval armor, a round plate protecting the interval between two pieces of plate-armor, as at the knee-joint or elbow-joint. {{smaller|During the period from the first introduction of plate in the earliest rerebrace to the complete suit of steel (nearly a century and a half), the protection of these joints was one of the most difficult problems, and the use of the roundel of steel (easy to forge and to attach), to protect the outer side of the elbow or knee, was almost universal; if it disappeared for a few years, it was only to come into use again. See ''roundel.''}}

'''bescutcheon''' (bē-skuch′o̤n), ''v. t.'' [< ''be-''<sup>1</sup> + ''scutcheon.''] To ornament with a scutcheon: as, “''bescutcheoned'' and betagged,” ''Churchill'', The Ghost, iv.

'''besee†''' (bē-sē′), ''v.'' [< ME. ''besen'', ''beseon'', ''biseon'', < AS. ''beseón'', look, look about (= OS. ''bisehan'', OFries. ''bisīa'' = Goth. ''bisaihwan''), < ''be-'' + ''seón'', see: see ''be-''<sup>1</sup> and ''see''<sup>1</sup>.] '''I.''' ''trans.'' '''1.''' To look at; see.—'''2.''' To look to; see to; attend to; arrange.—'''3.''' Reflexively, to look about one’s self; look to one’s self.

'''II.''' ''intrans.'' To look about; look.

'''beseech''' (bē-sēch′), ''v. t.''; pret. and pp. ''besought'', ppr. ''beseeching''. [Early mod. E. (north.) also ''beseek'', < ME. ''besechen'', ''bisechen'', also ''beseken'' (not in AS.) (= OFries. ''biseka'' = D. ''bezoeken'' = OHG. ''bisuochan'', MHG. ''besuochen'', G. ''besuchen'' = Sw. ''besōka'' = Dan. ''besöge'', visit, go to see), < ''be-'' + ''seken'', seek: see ''be-''<sup>1</sup> and ''seek.''] '''1.''' To entreat; supplicate; implore; ask or pray with urgency: followed by a personal object.
{{smaller block|I Paul myself ''beseech'' you by the meekness and gentleness of Christ.
{{right|2 Cor. x. 1.}}
<poem>I do ''beseech'' you
(Chiefly, that I might set it in my prayers),
What is your name?</poem>
{{right|''Shak.'', Tempest, iii. 1.}}}}
'''2.''' To beg eagerly for; solicit: followed by the thing solicited.
{{smaller block|<poem>But Eve . . . at his feet
Fell humble; and, embracing them, ''besought''</poem>}}

'''beseeming†''' (bẹ̄-sē′ming), ''n.'' Comeliness.

'''beseemingly''' (bẹ̄-sē′ming-li), ''adv.'' In a beseeming manner.

'''beseemingness''' (bẹ̄-sē′ming-nes), ''n.'' The quality of being beseeming.

'''beseemly†''' (bẹ̄-sēm′li), ''a.'' [< ''beseem'', confused with ''seemly''.] Seemly; fit; suitable: as, “''beseemly'' order,” ''Shenstone'', Schoolmistress.

'''beseen†''' (bẹ̄-sēn′), ''pp.'' [< ME. ''beseyn'', ''besein'', ''beseye'', ''byseyn'', etc., provided, arrayed, having a certain appearance, pp. of ''besen'', ''beseon'', besee: see ''besee''.] '''1.''' Seen; viewed; with reference to appearance, looking: as, a well-''beseen'' man.
{{smaller block|Arayd in . . . sad habiliments right well ''beseene''.
{{right|''Spenser'', F. Q., I. xii. 5.}}}}
Hence—'''2.''' Clad; arrayed; equipped.
{{smaller block|The Curate in his best ''beseene'' solemnly received him at the Churchyard stile.
{{right|''R. Carew'', Survey of Cornwall, p. 137 b.}}}}
'''3.''' Provided with as accomplishments; furnished.

'''beseke†''', ''v. t.'' A Middle English spelling of ''beseech''.

'''besenna''' (be-sen′ä), ''n.'' Same as ''mesenna''.

'''beset''' (bẹ̄-set′), ''v. t.''; pret. and pp. ''beset'', ppr. ''besetting''. [< ME. ''besetten'', ''bisetten'', < AS. ''besettan'' (= OFries. ''bisetta'' = D. ''bezetten'' = LG. '''berycid''' (ber′i-sid), ''n.'' A fish of the family ''Berycidæ.'' Also ''berycoid.''

'''Berycidæ''' (be-ris′i-dē), ''n. pl.''   [NL., < ''Beryx'' (''Beryc-'') + ''-idæ.'']   A family of acanthopterygian fishes, of which ''Beryx'' is the typical genus. {{smaller|Varying limits have been assigned to it. (''a'') In Günther’s sys-}}
{{smaller|tem it is the only family of the ''Beryciformes.'' (''b'') In Gill’s system it is limited to ''Berycoidea'', with a single dorsal fin having few spines in front, and ventral fins with many soft rays and moderate spines. It includes the genera ''Beryx'', ''Anoplogaster'', ''Caulolepis'', and others.}}

[[File:century v01 p0557 c1f1.png|center|329px]]
{{c|{{smaller|''Caulolepis longidens.''}}}}

'''beryciform''' (be-ris′i-fôrm), ''a.'' Having the characters of or pertaining to the ''Beryciformes.''

'''Beryciformes''' (be-ris-i-fôr′mēz), ''n. pl.''   [NL., < ''Beryx'' (''Beryc-'') + L. ''forma'', shape.]   In ''ichth.'', in Günther’s system of classification, the second division of the order ''Acanthopterygii'', characterized by a compressed oblong body, a head with large muciferous cavities covered with thin skin only, and the ventral fins thoracic with one spine and more than five soft rays (in ''Monocentris'' with only two).

'''II.''' ''n.'' Same as ''berycid.''

'''Beryllian''' (be-ril′ian), ''n.'' One of a sect founded in the third century by Beryllus, bishop of Bostra in Arabia, who taught that Christ was non-existent previous to his incarnation, and that at his birth a portion of the divine nature entered into him.

'''berylline''' (ber′i-lin), ''a.''   [< ''beryl'' + ''-ine''<sup>1</sup>.]   Like a beryl; of a light- or bluish-green color.

'''beryllium''' (be-ril′i-um), ''n.''   [NL., < Gr. βηρύλλιον, dim. of βήρυλλος, beryl.]   Same as ''glucinum''.

'''Berytus''' (be-rī′tus), ''n.''   [NL.]   A genus of hemipterous insects, typical of the family ''Berytidæ''.

'''Beryx''' (ber′iks), ''n.''   [NL.]   A genus of percoid fishes, typical of the family ''Berycidæ''.

'''berzeliite''' (bėr-zē′li-īt), ''n.''   [< ''Berzelius'' (see ''berzelianite'') + ''-ite''<sup>2</sup>.]   An arseniate of calcium, magnesium, and manganese occurring in honey-yellow masses, also less frequently in isometric crystals.

'''berzeline''' (bėr′ze-lin), ''n.''   [< ''Berzelius'' (see ''berzelianite'') + ''-ine''<sup>2</sup>.]   '''1.''' The copper selenide usually called ''berzelianite.''—'''2.''' A name early given to the mineral haüyne.

Also ''bessis.''

'''besabol''' (bes′ạ-bol), ''n.''   [Ar.]   A fragrant resinous balsam obtained from a burseraceous tree, ''Commiphora kataf'', of the Somali country in eastern Africa. {{smaller|It was formerly called ''East Indian myrrh'', and differs from true myrrh chiefly in its odor. Also ''bissabol.''}}

See ''roundel.''}}

'''besague''' (bes′ā-gū), ''n.''   [OF., also ''bisaiguë'', F. ''besaiguë'' = Pr. ''bezagudo'', < L. ''bis'', double, + {{img float|file=century v01 p0557 c2f1.png|width=230px|align=right|cap={{smaller|Besagues. (From Viollet-le-Duc’s “Dict. du Mobilier français.”)}}}} ''acuta'', ''acutus'', pointed, sharp: see ''bis-'' and ''acute'', and cf. E. ''twibill''.]   In ''medieval antiq.'': (''a'') A two-edged or two-pointed weapon, especially a sort of pick having one short point and one blunt or four-pointed head; a variety of the martel-de-fer (which see). (''b'') A carpenter’s tool with perhaps an ax-blade on one side and an adz-blade on the other.

'''besaint''' (bē-sānt′), ''v. t.''   [< ''be-''<sup>1</sup> + ''saint''.]   To make a saint of.
{{smaller block|Their canonizing . . . and ''besainting'' themselves.
{{right|''Hammond'', Works, IV. ix.}}}}

'''besant''', ''n.'' See ''bezant''.

'''bes-antler''', ''n.'' See ''bez-antler''.

'''besayle†''', ''n.''   [ME., < OF. ''besayel'', ''besaiol'' (F. ''bisaïeul''), a great-grandfather, < ''bes-'', ''bis-'' (< L. ''bis'', twice) + ''ayel'', ''aiol'', ''aïeul'', grandfather: see ''bis-'' and ''ayle''.]   A great-grandfather.—'''Writ of besayle''', {{smaller|in ''old law'', a writ by which a great-grandchild, wrongfully excluded from an ancestor’s property, vindicated his or her claim to it.}}

'''bescatter''' (bē-skat′ėr), ''v. t.''   [< ''be-''<sup>1</sup> + ''scatter''.]   To scatter over.
{{smaller block|With flowres ''bescattered''.
{{right|''Spenser'', F. Q., IV. xi. 46.}}}}

{{smaller block|The battlemented pine-''bescattered'' ridges on the further side.
{{right|''The Century'', XXVII. 39.}}}}

'''bescorn''' (bẹ̄-skôrn′), ''v. t.''   [< ''be-''<sup>1</sup> + ''scorn.'']   To treat with scorn; mock at.
{{smaller block|Then was he ''bescorned'' that onely should have been honoured in all things.
{{right|''Chaucer'', Parson’s Tale.}}}}

'''bescratch''' (bẹ̄-skrach′), ''v. t.''   [< ''be-''<sup>1</sup> + ''scratch.'']   To scratch; tear with the nails.   ''Spenser'', F. Q., III. v. 3.

'''bescrawl''' (bẹ̄-skrâl′), ''v. t.''   [< ''be-''<sup>1</sup> + ''scrawl.'']   To scrawl; scribble over.
{{smaller block|So far is it from the kenne of these wretched projectors of ours that ''bescraull'' their Pamflets every day with new formes of government for our Church.
{{right|''Milton'', Church-Government, i. 1.}}}}

'''bescreen''' (bẹ̄-skrēn′), ''v. t.''   [< ''be-''<sup>1</sup> + ''screen.'']   To cover with a screen, or as with a screen; shelter; conceal.
{{smaller block|''Bescreened'' in night.
{{right|''Shak.'', R. and J., ii. 2.}}}}

'''bescribble''' (bẹ̄-skrib′l), ''v. t.''   [< ''be-''<sup>1</sup> + ''scribble.'']   To scribble over.
{{smaller block|''Bescribbled'' with a thousand trifling impertinences.
{{right|''Milton'', Divorce, ii. 12.}}}}

'''bescumber†''' (bẹ̄-skum′bėr), ''v. t.''   [Also ''bescummer'', < ''be-''<sup>1</sup> + ''scumber'' or ''scummer.'']   To discharge ordure upon; befoul; besmear.   ''Marston.''
{{smaller block|<poem>Did Block ''bescumber''
Statute’s white suit with the parchment lace there?</poem>
{{right|''B. Jonson'', Staple of News, v. 2.}}}}
<poem>A critic that all the world ''bescumbers''
With satirical humours and lyrical numbers.</poem>
{{smaller block|{{right|''B. Jonson'', Poetaster, v. 1.}}}}

'''bescutcheon''' (bē-skuch′o̤n), ''v. t.''   [< ''be-''<sup>1</sup> + ''scutcheon.'']   To ornament with a scutcheon: as, “''bescutcheoned'' and betagged,” ''Churchill'', The Ghost, iv.

'''besee†''' (bē-sē′), ''v.''   [< ME. ''besen'', ''beseon'', ''biseon'', < AS. ''beseón'', look, look about (= OS. ''bisehan'', OFries. ''bisīa'' = Goth. ''bisaihwan''), < ''be-'' + ''seón'', see: see ''be-''<sup>1</sup> and ''see''<sup>1</sup>.]   '''I.''' ''trans.'' '''1.''' To look at; see.—'''2.''' To look to; see to; attend to; arrange.—'''3.''' Reflexively, to look about one’s self; look to one’s self.

'''II.''' ''intrans.'' To look about; look.

'''beseech''' (bē-sēch′), ''v. t.''; pret. and pp. ''besought'', ppr. ''beseeching''.   [Early mod. E. (north.) also ''beseek'', < ME. ''besechen'', ''bisechen'', also ''beseken'' (not in AS.) (= OFries. ''biseka'' = D. ''bezoeken'' = OHG. ''bisuochan'', MHG. ''besuochen'', G. ''besuchen'' = Sw. ''besōka'' = Dan. ''besöge'', visit, go to see), < ''be-'' + ''seken'', seek: see ''be-''<sup>1</sup> and ''seek.'']   '''1.''' To entreat; supplicate; implore; ask or pray with urgency: followed by a personal object.
{{smaller block|I Paul myself ''beseech'' you by the meekness and gentleness of Christ.
{{right|2 Cor. x. 1.}}}}
{{smaller block|<poem>I do ''beseech'' you
(Chiefly, that I might set it in my prayers),
What is your name?</poem>
{{right|''Shak.'', Tempest, iii. 1.}}}}
'''2.''' To beg eagerly for; solicit: followed by the thing solicited.
{{smaller block|<poem>But Eve . . . at his feet
Fell humble; and, embracing them, ''besought''</poem> His peace.{{right|''Milton'', P. L., x. 912.}}}}
{{smaller block|<poem>His sad eyes did ''beseech''
Some look from hers, so blind to him, so blind!</poem>{{right|''William Morris'', Earthly Paradise, II. 297.}}}}
{{smaller|='''Syn.''' ''Ask, Request, Beg'', etc. (see ''ask''), plead for or with, petition, conjure, appeal to.}}

'''beseech†''' (bẹ̄-sēch′), ''n.''   [< ''beseech, v.'']   A request: as, “such submiss ''beseeches,''” ''Fletcher (and others)'', Bloody Brother, iv. 2.

'''beseecher''' (bẹ̄-sē′chėr), ''n.'' One who beseeches.

'''beseechingly''' (bẹ̄-sē′ching-li), ''adv.'' In a beseeching manner.

'''beseechingness''' (bẹ̄-sē′ching-nes), ''n.'' The state or quality of being beseeching or earnestly solicitous.   ''George Eliot.''

'''beseechment''' (bẹ̄-sēch′ment), ''n.''   [< ''beseech'' + ''-ment.'']   The act of beseëching.   ''Goodwin.''

'''beseek†''' (bẹ̄-sēk′), ''v. t.'' Obsolete variant of ''beseech. Chaucer.''
{{smaller block|<poem>There with prayers meeke
And myld entreaty lodging did for her ''beseeke.''</poem>{{right|''Spenser'', F. Q., VI. iii. 37.}}}}

'''beseem''' (bẹ̄-sēm′), ''v.''   [< ME. ''besemen, bisemen,'' < ''be-'' + ''semen,'' seem: see ''be-''<sup>1</sup> and ''seem.'']   '''I.†''' ''intrans.'' '''1.''' To seem.
{{smaller block|As ''beseemed'' right.{{right|''Spenser'', F. Q., II. ix. 26.}}}}
'''2.''' To be seemly; be meet.

'''II.''' ''trans.'' '''1.''' To become; be fit for or worthy of.
{{smaller block|Grave, ''beseeming'' ornament.{{right|''Shak.'', R. and J., i. 1.}}}}
{{smaller block|In general, it has a quiet, didactic tone, such as ''beseems'' its subject and its age.{{right|''Ticknor'', Span. Lit., I. 91.}}}}
'''2†.''' To seem fit for.
{{smaller block|But foure of them the battell best ''beseemed.'' {{right|''Spenser'', F. Q., IV. ix. 20.}}}}

'''beseeming†''' (bẹ̄-sē′ming), ''n.'' Comeliness.

'''beseemingly''' (bẹ̄-sē′ming-li), ''adv.'' In a beseeming manner.

'''beseemingness''' (bẹ̄-sē′ming-nes), ''n.'' The quality of being beseeming.

'''beseemly†''' (bẹ̄-sēm′li), ''a.''   [< ''beseem'', confused with ''seemly''.]   Seemly; fit; suitable: as, “''beseemly'' order,” ''Shenstone'', Schoolmistress.

'''beseen†''' (bẹ̄-sēn′), ''pp.''   [< ME. ''beseyn'', ''besein'', ''beseye'', ''byseyn'', etc., provided, arrayed, having a certain appearance, pp. of ''besen'', ''beseon'', besee: see ''besee''.]   '''1.''' Seen; viewed; with reference to appearance, looking: as, a well-''beseen'' man.
{{smaller block|Arayd in . . . sad habiliments right well ''beseene''.
{{right|''Spenser'', F. Q., I. xii. 5.}}}}
Hence—'''2.''' Clad; arrayed; equipped.
{{smaller block|The Curate in his best ''beseene'' solemnly received him at the Churchyard stile.
{{right|''R. Carew'', Survey of Cornwall, p. 137 b.}}}}
'''3.''' Provided with as accomplishments; furnished.

'''beseke†''', ''v. t.'' A Middle English spelling of ''beseech''.

'''besenna''' (be-sen′ä), ''n.'' Same as ''mesenna''.
